218.title: Pauri 33, sound: aakhan jor
218.tomorrow: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own
218.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33's repeated word jor, power, gives it a strong, hammering rhythm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pavarreeaa, the steps, and your line, step by step. Today, the next rung, sound first.

Ever tried not to laugh? A quiet classroom, a serious meeting, a moment when laughing is the worst thing you could do. And it rises anyway. You bite your cheek, you stare at the floor, and your shoulders shake. Or the opposite: you want to say the right thing to a grieving friend, and nothing comes out at all. Speaking and staying quiet look like the two things a person controls best. Pauri 33 opens with exactly those two, and one hard little word that keeps coming back like a hammer.
screen: `TRYING NOT TO LAUGH.` → `THE WORDS THAT WON'T COME.` → `ONE WORD, LIKE A HAMMER.`

segments.voice: The first line: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Four sounds. Aakhan: speaking, saying; it echoes aakheeah from yesterday, where the Name was said on a million tongues. Jor: power, force, strength, still alive in everyday Punjabi when people mean push hard, put your strength into it. Chupai: in silence; you may know chup from Punjabi, as in chup kar, be quiet. Nah: not, no. So: no power to speak, no power to keep silent. Commentators read that nah across both halves. Now the shape. Jor lands at the end of each half: two short beats, then the heavy one. The next line flips it, so jor comes first and last: jor na mangan, den na jor. No power to ask, no power to give. The word boxes the line in. The whole stanza keeps doing this: jor ten times in eight short lines, nine of them with na or nah beside it, like knocking on door after door and finding each one locked. Tomorrow, which doors, and whose hand holds the key. Today, feel the hammer. You can almost recite this stanza by its rhythm alone.
screen: `AAKHAN — SPEAKING.` · `JOR — POWER, FORCE.` · `CHUPAI NAH JOR — NOR TO BE SILENT.` · `JOR, AGAIN AND AGAIN, LIKE A HAMMER.` · then, large: `AAKHAN JOR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud three times, slowly, letting jor land heavy like a hand on a table: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor; then the next one, jor na mangan, den na jor. Then stop speaking and simply stay silent. Even the silence isn't quite yours, since thoughts keep talking; don't fight them, let them knock and pass.
Chupai, silence. It opens: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor, no power to speak, no power to be silent, and the word jor keeps coming back like a hammer.
Your line: aakhan jor. Even speech and silence aren't fully in our power. Until tomorrow.

219.title: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own
219.hook: no power to speak or be silent, to live or die, to beg or give; the power is in His hand (Japji 33)
219.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33 is commonly taught as a stanza against haumai, the ego that claims its own power, and its last line, no one is high or low, is often linked with Sikh teaching on equality.

segments.voice: Yesterday: chupai, silence, and your line, aakhan jor: no power to speak, none to be silent. Today, the whole stanza.

Ask anyone who has taught a teenager to drive about the phantom brake. In the passenger seat, the teacher's right foot presses hard into the floor, again and again, where no pedal exists. A hand grips the door handle. The whole body is trying to steer a car it isn't driving. It doesn't help. It just wears them out. Plenty of people ride through life like that, gripping the outcome of the interview, the test results, the way the kids turn out. Pauri 33 walks through almost everything a person might think they control, and taps on each one.
screen: `THE PHANTOM BRAKE.` → `GRIPPING WHAT YOU DON'T DRIVE.` → `PAURI 33 TAPS ON EACH ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, in paraphrase. No power to speak, none to keep silent. None to ask, none to give. None to live, none to die. No power to hold on to kingdoms and wealth, the things that set the mind clamoring. None over awareness, knowledge or reflection. And one last knock on the yogis' door: no power in any technique, any jugat, to get free of the world on our own. Then the hand that holds what we don't: jis hath jor kar vekhai soe. The One in whose hand the power is, does it, and watches over it. And the final line: Nanak utam neech na koe. By themselves, no one is high and no one is low. Two things to notice. First, this isn't a stanza about giving up. A stanza ago, Japji pictured a climb step by step, and Sikh life is full of honest work and service. Sikh teachers read Pauri 33 as aimed at haumai, the ego that says I did this, all by myself. The effort is yours to make. The power behind it isn't yours to own. Second, where it lands. If nobody's power is their own, nobody gets to stand above anybody else. The king with his treasury and the beggar with his bowl hold exactly the same amount of jor. It begins as letting go and ends as equality.
screen: `NO POWER TO SPEAK, ASK, LIVE, OR DIE.` · `NOT EVEN IN A TECHNIQUE.` · `THE POWER IS IN HIS HAND.` · `SO NO ONE IS HIGH OR LOW.` · then, large: `NOT IN MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're gripping right now, a result you're waiting for, a person you're worried about, a plan that might not work, and notice where the grip sits: jaw, shoulders, hands, stomach. Open your hands, palms up, on your lap; you're not giving up on it, just taking your foot off a brake that isn't there. Breathe out, let the shoulders drop, and stay with open hands.
Haumai, the ego that says I did this alone. No power of our own to speak or be silent, to live or die, to ask or give; the power is in His hand, and so no one is high and no one is low.
Your line: not in my hands. The effort is yours; the power never was. Day two hundred nineteen, done.

220.title: Pauri 34, sound: raatee rutee
220.tomorrow: Pauri 34, meaning: a place for dharma
220.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 34 begins the stanzas many teachers describe as the realms, opening with a line that names night, season, lunar day and weekday.

segments.voice: Yesterday: haumai, the ego, and your line, not in my hands. Today, a new stanza, and it starts with time itself.

A calendar hangs on the kitchen wall in many Punjabi homes. It isn't just days and months. In small type are the moon's phases, the full-moon days, the first day of each month when many families go to the gurdwara. Grandparents read it like the weather: this is a good day for that, the full moon is Thursday. Time, on that wall, has layers. The night, the season, the moon, the day of the week, all stacked on top of each other. Pauri 34 opens with that stack, four words long, and it sounds like a clock ticking.
screen: `A CALENDAR ON THE KITCHEN WALL.` → `TIME, IN LAYERS.` → `FOUR WORDS, LIKE A CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Raatee rutee thitee vaar. Four words, four kinds of time. Raatee: nights. Rutee: seasons; a rut is a season, the way the monsoon or the cold season comes around. Thitee: lunar days. A thit is one day of the moon's month, counted from new moon to full, the small print on that kitchen calendar. Vaar: the days of the week, still heard in weekday names across North India: Somvaar, Mangalvaar, and so on. In four words, Nanak lays down the whole clock: night, season, moon, week. Now the sound. Raatee, rutee, thitee: the same shape, a short first beat and a long ee, like three ticks. Then vaar, open and long, like the chime. Then the line turns from time to things: pavan paanee aganee paataal. Air, water, fire, and the regions below. Pavan, paanee: two p's, soft as breath. Aganee: fire, a cousin of the Sanskrit agni. Paataal: the underworlds, the depths. First the clock, then the elements. Tomorrow, what Nanak sets in the middle of all this, and the job he gives it.
screen: `RAATEE, RUTEE — NIGHTS, SEASONS.` · `THITEE, VAAR — MOON-DAYS, WEEKDAYS.` · `THREE TICKS AND A CHIME.` · `PAVAN PAANEE AGANEE — AIR, WATER, FIRE.` · then, large: `RAATEE RUTEE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud three times, raatee rutee thitee vaar, pavan paanee aganee paataal: tick on the first three words, chime on vaar, then let the second half flow like breath. Afterward, sit and notice what time it is for you, in layers: day or night, which season outside, which day of the week. Let the answers come and settle, and breathe.
Thitee, the lunar days. It opens with the whole clock in four words, nights, seasons, moon-days and weekdays, and then the elements: air, water, fire and the depths.
Your line: raatee rutee, nights and seasons. The whole clock fits in four words. Two hundred twenty days now.

221.title: Pauri 34, meaning: a place for dharma
221.hook: nights, seasons and days, air, water and fire, and in their midst the earth set as a home for right action (Japji 34)
221.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 34 is taught as the first of the five khands, or realms, and its picture of the earth as a dharamsaal is often drawn on to describe ordinary life as the place for right action.

segments.voice: Yesterday: thitee, the lunar days, and your line, raatee rutee, nights and seasons. Today, what Nanak sets in the middle of all that time.

Every room you walk into tells you what it's for. A gym is for sweating. A library is for quiet. A kitchen is for feeding people. The rules come with the room, even if no one says them. Nobody jogs through a library or reads novels on the bench press. Now zoom all the way out. What if someone told you what the whole earth is for? Not what it's made of or how old it is, but what it's for. Pauri 34 answers that in one line.
screen: `A GYM, A LIBRARY, A KITCHEN.` → `EVERY PLACE HAS A PURPOSE.` → `WHAT IS THE EARTH FOR?`

segments.voice: After the frame, nights, seasons, moon-days, weekdays, air, water, fire and the depths, comes the line it was built for: tis vich dharatee thaap rakhee dharam saal. In the middle of it all, He set the earth down as a dharamsaal, a house for dharma. Dharma here means right action, living rightly, doing what is true. The earth isn't pictured as a waiting room or a prison. It's a place built for doing good. The word lives outside this stanza too: Sikh tradition remembers the early places where Sikhs gathered to sing and eat together as dharamsals, before gurdwara became the usual word. Then the stanza fills the house. Beings of every kind and color live there, with names beyond counting. Karmee karmee hoe veechaar: each one is weighed by their own deeds. True is the One, and true the court. There the accepted ones shine, and by grace they receive the mark. Kach pakaaee othai paae: there the unripe and the ripe are sorted, like fruit. Nanak says, go there and you'll see. The next stanza names this realm: Dharam Khand. Khand is a region, a realm, the first of five Japji describes: dharma, knowledge, effort, grace and truth, rising like floors of a house. And the first floor is right here, under your feet.
screen: `THE EARTH, SET AS A DHARAMSAAL.` · `DHARMA — RIGHT ACTION.` · `EACH WEIGHED BY THEIR DEEDS.` · `THE FIRST OF FIVE REALMS.` · then, large: `DHARAM KHAND.`

segments.voice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel the ground holding you: the dharamsaal, the house built for right action. Choose one right thing, small and real, a call you owe, a mess to clean up, an honest answer, a kindness no one expects, and picture yourself doing it clearly. Then let the picture go, keep your feet on the ground, and breathe.
Dharam Khand. The realm of dharma: this earth, set in the middle of time and the elements as a house for right action. The first of Japji's five realms.
Your line: the earth is for dharma. Ordinary life is where right action lives. See you tomorrow.

222.title: Pauri 35, sound: dharam khandd kaa
222.tomorrow: Pauri 35, meaning: the realm of knowledge
222.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 35 opens with a line that closes the realm of dharma and opens the realm of knowledge, then repeats kete, so many, through the rest of the stanza.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dharam Khand, the realm of right action, and your line, the earth is for dharma. Today, the sound of the stanza that names it.
screen: `DHARAM KHAND — THE EARTH IS FOR DHARMA.`

segments.voice: On a train, a voice comes over the speaker: this stop, Central. Next stop, Riverside. One sentence, two jobs. It closes the station you're pulling out of and names the one ahead. Nobody has to look out the window to know the trip has moved on. Pauri 35 opens with a sentence built just like that, a hinge between two places. And as soon as the next place comes into view, one small word starts repeating, as if the speaker keeps turning around and finding more.
screen: `THIS STOP.` → `NEXT STOP.` → `A HINGE BETWEEN TWO PLACES.`

segments.voice: The hinge: dharam khandd kaa eho dharam, giaan khandd kaa aakhahu karam. First half. Dharam khandd: the realm of dharma, yesterday's word, sung with a strong double d at the end, khandd. Kaa: of. Eho: this, this very. Dharam: dharma. So: this is the dharma of the realm of dharma. That's this stop, closing behind us: the earth as a house for right action, each weighed by their deeds. Second half. Giaan khandd: the realm of knowledge. You met giaan in Pauri 29, wisdom as the meal. Kaa: of. Aakhahu: tell, speak of it; you can hear aakhan from Pauri 33 in it. Karam: here, the doings, the workings. So: now tell of the workings of the realm of knowledge. That's the next stop. The two halves rhyme on their last words: dharam, karam. Then comes the word that repeats: kete, how many, so many. Kete pavan paanee vaisantar: so many winds, waters and fires. Kete, kete, kete, line after line, more than a dozen times by the end of the stanza. Tomorrow, what's being counted.

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud three times, feeling the first half close and the second half open: dharam khandd kaa eho dharam, giaan khandd kaa aakhahu karam. Then sit in the pause at a station, doors open, one stop behind you with everything you already know, and something larger ahead. Don't move yet; stay in the pause and breathe.
Kete, so many, how many. It opens with a hinge: this is the way of the realm of dharma; now tell of the realm of knowledge, and the word kete begins.
Your line: dharam khandd. One realm closes as the next one opens. That's day two hundred twenty-two.

223.title: Pauri 35, meaning: the realm of knowledge
223.hook: beyond duty is the realm of knowledge: winds, waters, suns and worlds without number (Japji 35)
223.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 35 is taught as the realm of knowledge, the second of the five khands, and its long list of kete, so many, is often read as the ego opening up before the vastness of creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kete, so many, and your line, dharam khandd, the hinge between two realms. Today, through into the realm of knowledge.

Astronomers once pointed a space telescope at a tiny patch of sky that looked completely empty. Dark. Nothing there. They left the camera open a long time, collecting whatever faint light trickled in. When the picture came back, that empty patch was full of galaxies, each one a city of stars. A picture like that can make the floor drop away. The universe is bigger than anyone can hold in mind. Japji has a name for the place where that dizziness lives, and it got there with no telescope at all: the realm of knowledge.
screen: `AN EMPTY PATCH OF SKY.` → `FULL OF GALAXIES.` → `THE FLOOR DROPS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Gian Khand. In the first realm, you learn to live rightly on this earth. In the second, your eyes open to how big everything actually is. Nanak shows it by counting, and failing to finish. Kete, so many. So many winds, waters and fires. So many lands where deeds are done, so many great mountains. So many moons, so many suns, so many worlds and lands. He reaches for figures his listeners honored, the creator Brahma, Krishna, Shiva, the great teachers and sages, and says there are so many of them too. The point isn't to make anyone small. It's to show how big the whole is. Then the list turns to us: so many ways life begins, so many languages, so many kings, so many kinds of awareness, so many who serve. And the stanza ends: Nanak ant na ant. There is no end to its end. Knowledge here isn't a pile of facts. It's the moment the facts become too many to hold, and the heart goes quiet in wonder. Some Sikh teachers say this realm breaks the small self open: you can't stay the center of the world once you've seen how many worlds there are. In the stanza, that isn't a loss. It's where wonder starts.

224.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 36 opens with giaan khandd meh giaan parchandd, still in the realm of knowledge, before the stanza turns to the realm of effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gian Khand, the realm of knowledge, and your line: so many worlds. Today, the end of a week, and the start of the last climb.

A bonfire at night. Not a candle: a fire so bright the faces around it glow and the dark beyond goes darker. Nobody near it looks anywhere else. Pauri 36 begins with a line that burns like that. First, look back down this week's ladder. Aakhan jor: no power to speak, none to be silent, the power not in my hands. Raatee rutee: nights and seasons, the whole clock. The earth set down as a house for right action, for dharma. Dharam khandd, the hinge. And yesterday, so many worlds. Six rungs. Now the Japji enters its last stretch: three more stanzas and a final salok.
screen: `A BONFIRE AT NIGHT.` → `A WEEK: NOT IN MY HANDS, THE CLOCK, DHARMA.` → `A LINE THAT BURNS.`

segments.voice: Pauri 36 opens: giaan khandd meh giaan parchandd. Giaan khandd: the realm of knowledge, the one you walked into yesterday. Meh: in. Giaan: knowledge. Parchandd: blazing, fierce, like a fire at full strength or the sun at noon. In the realm of knowledge, knowledge blazes. Hear how the line doubles its word: giaan, then giaan again, the second one on fire, as if the word itself catches light. Then: tithai naad binod kodd anand. Tithai: there. Naad: the sound, the note, the same word from Pauri 29, sounding in every heart. Binod: play, delight. Kodd: ten million, a crore, a number too big to picture. Anand: joy, bliss. There, music, play, and joy by the millions. Now the rhyme that holds the two lines together: parchandd, anand. The fire, then the joy. The first line is bright and hard, with that strong dd at the end; the second is soft and wide, ending on an open breath. Tomorrow the stanza turns to a new realm. For now, notice what Nanak puts inside a realm of knowledge. Not lecture halls. Music, play and joy.

segments.voice: Say the first two lines aloud, slowly, three times: giaan khandd meh giaan parchandd, tithai naad binod kodd anand, the first bright and firm, the second soft and wide. Then sit quietly and picture warm light in the center of your chest, steady, like a flame out of the wind. Let it glow as you breathe, with nothing to think about.
Parchandd, blazing. It opens in the realm of knowledge, where knowledge blazes, and there is music, play and joy by the millions.
Your line: giaan khandd, the realm of knowledge. Where knowledge blazes, there is music too. A week, done.
